content: Frostbite is a type of thermal injury that occurs when tissues are exposed to sub-zero temperatures (in degrees Celsius) for a prolonged period, leading to the formation of ice crystals within the affected tissues. Depending on the extent of tissue damage, complications such as thrombosis (blood clot formation), ischaemia (restricted blood flow), necrosis (tissue death), gangrene, and, in severe cases, the need for amputation may arise. Various treatments have been proposed for frostbite injuries, including hyperbaric oxygen therapy, sympathectomy (a nerve-blocking procedure), thrombolytic therapy (to dissolve blood clots), and the use of vasodilating agents such as iloprost, reserpine, pentoxifylline, and buflomedil. However, the effectiveness and safety of these interventions remain uncertain. To evaluate the potential benefits and harms of different frostbite management strategies, a systematic review was conducted. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and trial registries up to November 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing any medical intervention (e.g., pharmacological treatments, topical therapies, or rewarming techniques) to another treatment, placebo, or no treatment were included. One open-label randomized trial involving 47 participants with severe frostbite injuries met the inclusion criteria. All participants underwent rapid rewarming and received 250 mg of aspirin and 400 mg of intravenous (IV) buflomedil (a drug that has since been withdrawn from clinical use). They were then randomized into three treatment groups for an eight-day period: 1. Group 1 received an additional 400 mg of IV buflomedil for one hour per day. 2. Group 2 received IV iloprost (a prostacyclin analog) at a dose of 0.5 ng to 2 ng/kg/min for six hours per day. 3. Group 3 received IV iloprost at 2 ng/kg/min for six hours per day, combined with fibrinolysis using 100 mg of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) on the first day only. The results suggested that iloprost, as well as iloprost combined with rtPA, may reduce the rate of amputations in individuals with severe frostbite compared to buflomedil alone. Specifically: Iloprost alone reduced the risk of amputation with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.05 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.00 to 0.78; P = 0.03), based on very low-quality evidence. Iloprost combined with rtPA also reduced the risk of amputation with an RR of 0.31 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.94; P = 0.04), again based on very low-quality evidence. Iloprost alone may be as effective as iloprost combined with rtPA in reducing amputation rates, with an RR of 0.14 (95% CI 0.01 to 2.56; P = 0.19), though this evidence is also of very low quality. No deaths or withdrawals due to adverse events were reported in any of the treatment groups, but the quality of evidence for these outcomes was very low. Adverse events, such as flushing, nausea, palpitations, and vomiting, were commonly reported but were not analyzed separately for each treatment group. The study did not assess other important outcomes, such as acute pain, chronic pain, ability to perform daily activities, quality of life, or occupational effects. In conclusion, there is a significant lack of high-quality evidence regarding the treatment of frostbite injuries. Limited and very low-quality evidence from a single small trial suggests that iloprost, either alone or in combination with rtPA, may reduce the need for amputation in severe frostbite cases compared to buflomedil alone. However, given that buflomedil is no longer in clinical use and the evidence is of very low quality, further high-quality randomized trials are urgently needed to establish effective treatments for frostbite injuries.
